title: Water at the molecular frontier
authors: Mischa Bonn, Marie-Laure Bocquet, Andre Geim, Laura Fumagalli, Angelos Michaelides, Lyderic Bocquet
abstract: Much of the water that matters most - flowing through biological cells and membranes, percolating through soils and rocks, or processed by filtration and desalination technologies - is not bulk water. It is water in nano- and molecular-scale confinement or at interfaces. Nanoscale water is therefore central to many challenges of our time, from the global water crisis and the water-energy nexus to catalysis, electrochemistry, and health. Beyond its applications, nanoscale water has emerged as a rich scientific field in its own right: discoveries are accumulating rapidly, revealing that confinement and interfacial forces produce a range of behaviours absent in the bulk. Sometimes this amounts to a renormalization of bulk properties; in other cases, new and non-intuitive phenomena emerge - exotic phases, anomalous transport, and dielectric responses that defy continuum expectations. A convergence of atomically precise nanofluidic devices, novel spectroscopies and microscopy approaches, and machine-learning-accelerated simulations is now exposing the molecular mechanisms behind these behaviours. This Perspective argues that the recent findings should not be viewed as isolated nanoscale anomalies, but as evidence for a molecular regime of water in which continuum descriptions must be rethought and molecular-level understanding becomes essential. Recognising and exploring this regime should have consequences ranging from fundamental physics to the rational design of future technologies that rely on water and dissolved ions.
summary: This perspective reviews the emerging field of water physics at the molecular frontier, where confinement in nano-channels drastically alters properties compared to bulk water. By integrating data from advanced spectroscopy, nanofluidics, and machine-learning simulations, the authors argue that a fundamental molecular understanding is needed to predict and engineer water-based technologies. This work is crucial for understanding everything from desalination to biological function.
main_problem: The central challenge is understanding the physical properties of water when confined to nano- and molecular-scale environments, as bulk continuum models fail to capture the true behavior.
main_result: Water exhibits complex, confinement-dependent behaviors—ranging from structural reshaping and anomalous transport to dielectric anisotropy—requiring a molecular-level understanding that goes beyond simple renormalization of bulk properties.
method: The field advances through a convergence of atomically precise nanofluidic experiments, advanced spectroscopies (like SFG), and high-fidelity simulations utilizing machine-learning potentials.
model_or_system: The focus is on water confined in various nanoscale geometries, such as graphene slits, nanopores, and biological membranes. The models range from continuum hydrodynamics to atomistic molecular dynamics simulations.
key_observables: Structure, dynamics, dielectric response ($\epsilon_{\perp}, \epsilon_{\parallel}$), ionic conductivity ($\sigma$), and hydrogen-bond dynamics.
important_parameters: Confinement strength (pore width), wall material properties (compliance), and temperature/pressure regimes.
main_assumptions: The paper argues against viewing nanoscale effects as isolated anomalies, suggesting a unified molecular regime must be established.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crossover between interface-dominated and confinement-dominated regimes, showing predicted phase diagrams and measured dielectric constant deviations.
paper_structure: The perspective reviews the limitations of bulk theories, presents evidence from multiple experimental and simulation platforms (nanofluidics, spectroscopy, ML simulations), and concludes by outlining the necessity of a molecular-level framework.
why_interesting: The study of water's dielectric response and ion transport under extreme confinement touches upon non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and complex many-body dynamics, offering insights into how boundary conditions fundamentally alter bulk material properties.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Several important water-related technologies rely on the molecular properties of nanoscale water, including water purification, desalination, selective ion transport, and hydrogen generation from water. Despite the apparent technological impact of understanding nanoscale water, many fundamental insights are lacking. A fundamental, molecular-level understanding of nanoscale water is expected to enable novel, clever technologies beyond the current capabilities. We argue that the bottleneck for new technologies is our limited understanding of nanoscale water.
